problem: Consider a spherical planet with radius $(2\times {10}^{7})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=20\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of $(6\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m/s},$ where $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.

examples.problem: Consider a spherical planet with radius $(8\times10^5)\,\textrm{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g = 16\,\textrm{m/s}^2.$ Which equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of $(9\times10^{4})\,\textrm{m/s},$ where $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
examples.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be the planet's radius and $g$ be the planet's surface gravitational acceleration.

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
F_\text{in} = G\,\dfrac{mM}{r^2},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-F_\textrm{in}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, 

$$
a=-\dfrac{k}{r^2},
$$

 with constant of proportionality $k=GM > 0.$

When at the surface, $r=R,$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-g.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k{:}$

$$
-g = -\dfrac{k}{R^2} 
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
k = gR^2
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a = -\dfrac{gR^2}{r^2}.
$$

Now, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}r} = -\dfrac{gR^2}{r^2}
$$

Solving using separation of variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\frac{dv}{dr}\,dr & =\int (-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}})\,dr \\ \int v\,dv & =-g{R}^{2}\int \frac{1}{{r}^{2}}\,dr \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2} & =-g{R}^{2}(-\frac{1}{r})+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C=2C_1$ is a constant of integration.

Let $v_0$ be the initial velocity of the object. Applying the initial condition $v(R) = v_0,$ we can solve for $C{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(R)^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{R}+C \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =2gR+C \\ C & ={v}_{0}^{2}-2gR\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation for the velocity of the object is

$$
v^2 = \dfrac{2gR^2}{r} + v_0^2 - 2gR.
$$

Finally, substituting in the values
$R=(8\times10^5),$
$g=16,$ and
$v_0=(9\times10^{4}),$
we conclude that the equation for the velocity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2\cdot 16\cdot (8\times {10}^{5})^{2}}{r}+(9\times {10}^{4})^{2}-2\cdot 16\cdot (8\times {10}^{5}) \\  & =\frac{2048\times {10}^{10}}{r}+(81\times {10}^{8})-(256\times {10}^{5}) \\  & =\frac{2.048\times {10}^{13}}{r}+(8.1\times {10}^{9})-(0.0256\times {10}^{9}) \\  & =\frac{2.048\times {10}^{13}}{r}+((8.1-0.0256)\times {10}^{9}) \\  & =\frac{2.048\times {10}^{13}}{r}+(8.0744\times {10}^{9}).\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem: Consider a spherical rocky planet with radius $(5.8\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=7.5\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which differential equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the rocky planet, where $r$ is the distance from the rocky planet's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
feedback.worked_solution:
According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the rocky planet is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the rocky planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=(5.8\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m},$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-7.5\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-7.5 & =-\frac{k}{(5.8\times {10}^{4})^{2}} \\ k & =7.5\cdot (5.8\times {10}^{4})^{2} \\  & =7.5\cdot (5.8)^{2}\times ({10}^{4})^{2} \\  & =252.3\times {10}^{8} \\  & =2.523\times {10}^{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{2.523\times {10}^{10}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{2.523\times {10}^{10}}{{r}^{2}}
$$
